topics.summary: Input iterators support single-pass reading under their contracts. Forward iterators support multipass traversal. blocks.text: These distinctions explain why std::distance can be constant time for a vector yet linear for a forward list. A binary-search algorithm can use logarithmic comparisons on a forward range while still performing substantial iterator movement. Complexity must count the relevant operations, not assume every increment or midpoint access has the same cost.

blocks.text: Iterator categories express capabilities and complexity expectations. An input iterator can be single-pass: copying it does not necessarily create an independent reusable traversal of the same source. A forward iterator supports multipass use under its contract. Bidirectional and random-access iterators add movement operations, while contiguous iterators connect traversal to contiguous storage.
rich: Iterator categories express capabilities and complexity expectations. An input iterator can be single-pass: copying it does not necessarily create an independent reusable traversal of the same source. A forward iterator supports multipass use under its contract. Bidirectional and random-access iterators add movement operations, while contiguous iterators connect traversal to contiguous storage.

blocks.text: The category affects algorithm choice. std::distance over a vector can obtain a distance without visiting every element. Over a forward list it advances through the sequence. A binary-search algorithm on forward iterators can reduce the number of comparisons logarithmically while still performing linear-scale iterator movement. Counting comparisons alone can therefore misrepresent actual work.

blocks.text: Do not upgrade an iterator’s category just because one operation is easy to implement in a teaching wrapper. A claimed category promises a family of behavior and complexity properties. Library algorithms may rely on those promises. An iterator that advertises random access but performs every jump through a linear scan defeats the advertised complexity model even if small tests return correct values.

Selecting a container and selecting an algorithm are connected decisions, not independent checklist items.

Increasing size within capacity may avoid relocating existing elements, while growing beyond capacity requires new storage under the usual vector operation model. blocks.text: Erasing can invalidate the erased position and later positions, including an old end iterator under the vector rules. Recompute through the returned state rather than carrying a stale cached endpoint into a mutating loop. Other containers have different guarantees, so read the specific operation contract instead of memorizing one global rule for all iterators.

blocks.text: The erase loop has two transitions. When an element is removed, erase returns the next valid position and the loop assigns it directly. When an element is kept, the loop increments the current iterator. Incrementing again after erasure would skip the element that shifted into the erased position. Retaining the old iterator would instead use invalid traversal state.

blocks.text: Other containers have different invalidation rules. Erasing one list node does not invalidate iterators to unrelated nodes. An unordered-container rehash invalidates iterators but does not by itself invalidate references or pointers to existing elements under the standard’s specified guarantees. A vector erase affects positions at and after the erased location. Memorizing one rule for “containers” is not sufficient.

blocks.text: A stable iterator is not a stable business relationship. A node can remain alive while its value changes, and a pointer can remain valid while the application has logically retired the record. Conversely, a stable identifier can name a record that now lives at a different address. Match the handle to the requirement: traversal position, object lifetime, or domain identity.

Sanitizers and debug iterators can catch some invalid uses, but the absence of a diagnostic does not grant permission to use stale state.

Retaining the old iterator would instead use invalid traversal state.

Other containers have different invalidation rules. Erasing one list node does not invalidate iterators to unrelated nodes. An unordered-container rehash invalidates iterators but does not by itself invalidate references or pointers to existing elements under the standard’s specified guarantees. A vector erase affects positions at and after the erased location. Memorizing one rule for “containers” is not sufficient.

A stable iterator is not a stable business relationship. A node can remain alive while its value changes, and a pointer can remain valid while the application has logically retired the record. Conversely, a stable identifier can name a record that now lives at a different address. Match the handle to the requirement: traversal position, object lifetime, or domain identity.

Tests should never prove validity by dereferencing an iterator after an operation known to invalidate it. Reacquire a valid handle and compare logical values. Sanitizers and debug iterators can catch some invalid uses, but the absence of a diagnostic does not grant permission to use stale state.

blocks.text: The loop’s two branches encode its invariant: the current iterator always identifies the next unclassified element or the current end. This reasoning scales better than trying to patch skipped values after a fragile loop has already run.
